Apple___Apple_scab.summary: Apple scab causes olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit. It spreads in cool, wet spring weather and can cause early leaf fall and cracked, unmarketable fruit.
immediate_steps: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves and fruit.
Rake and destroy fallen leaves under the tree so spores do not survive.
Start a protective spray round before the next rain.
prevention: Prune to open the canopy so leaves dry quickly.
Spray at green-tip and petal-fall stages in scab-prone areas.
Prefer scab-tolerant varieties for new planting.
organic_options: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L before rain periods.
Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L at bud break (not during bloom).
chemical_options: Captan 50 WP @ 2.5 g/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L as protectants.
Difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.3 ml/L or hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L after infection periods.
Apple___Apple_scab.irrigation_tip: Use basin or drip irrigation; avoid sprinklers that wet the foliage.
Apple___Apple_scab.weather_watch: High risk when leaves stay wet for 9+ hours at 15-24 °C, especially during spring rains.

Apple___Black_rot.summary: Black rot produces purple-bordered 'frog-eye' leaf spots, sunken cankers on branches and rotting, mummified fruit. The fungus survives in dead wood and old fruit.
immediate_steps: Cut out cankered branches 15 cm below visible damage and burn them.
Remove mummified fruit from the tree and ground.
Disinfect pruning tools between cuts.
prevention: Keep trees vigorous with balanced nutrition; stressed trees are more susceptible.
Remove dead wood every dormant season.
Protect large pruning wounds with a copper or Bordeaux paste.
organic_options: Bordeaux mixture 1% at dormant stage.
Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L after pruning.
chemical_options: Captan 50 WP @ 2.5 g/L from petal fall at 10-14 day intervals.
Thiophanate-methyl 70 WP @ 1 g/L where approved.
Apple___Black_rot.irrigation_tip: Water deeply at the root zone during dry spells to avoid drought stress.
Apple___Black_rot.weather_watch: Warm (20-30 °C), humid and rainy periods during fruit development favour infection.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.summary: Cedar apple rust forms bright yellow-orange spots on leaves and fruit. The fungus needs juniper/cedar trees nearby to complete its life cycle.
immediate_steps: Remove heavily infected leaves where practical.
Look for and remove galls on nearby juniper or cedar trees.
Apply a protective fungicide before the next wet period.
prevention: Avoid planting junipers within a few hundred metres of apple orchards.
Plant rust-resistant apple varieties.
Spray from pink bud through petal fall in rust-prone years.
organic_options: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L as a protectant.
chemical_options: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L as a protectant.
Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 0.5 g/L or hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.irrigation_tip: Irrigate at soil level in the morning so foliage stays dry.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.weather_watch: Spring rains with 13-24 °C temperatures release spores from juniper galls.

Apple___healthy.summary: The apple leaf looks healthy. Keep up regular orchard care and scout weekly, especially before and after rains.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Continue weekly scouting of leaves and young fruit.
Keep the orchard floor clean of fallen leaves.
prevention: Prune annually for good light and airflow.
Apply balanced NPK and farmyard manure based on a soil test.
Use protective sprays only when local disease forecasts warn of scab or rust.
organic_options: Mulch the basin with organic matter to conserve moisture.
Neem cake in the basin to support soil health.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Apple___healthy.irrigation_tip: Irrigate at 7-10 day intervals in dry weather using basin or drip; avoid waterlogging.
Apple___healthy.weather_watch: Watch for prolonged leaf wetness in spring, which raises scab risk.

Blueberry___healthy.summary: The blueberry leaf looks healthy. Blueberries need acidic, well-drained soil and steady moisture.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout weekly for leaf spots and pests.
Remove weak or dead canes.
prevention: Keep soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5.
Mulch with pine needles or sawdust.
Prune old canes in winter to keep bushes open.
organic_options: Organic mulch and compost to maintain soil acidity and moisture.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Blueberry___healthy.irrigation_tip: Keep soil evenly moist with drip irrigation; blueberry roots are shallow.
Blueberry___healthy.weather_watch: Hot, dry spells stress plants; warm humid weather raises fungal leaf spot risk.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.summary: Powdery mildew forms white powdery patches on young leaves and shoots, causing curling and reduced growth. Unlike most fungi it thrives in warm, dry days with humid nights.
immediate_steps: Prune out heavily infected shoot tips.
Start sulphur sprays at the first white patches.
Avoid excess nitrogen that produces soft, susceptible growth.
prevention: Prune for an open canopy and good airflow.
Remove suckers and water sprouts, which get infected first.
Spray protectively in orchards with a history of mildew.
organic_options: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L (do not spray above 32 °C).
Potassium bicarbonate @ 5 g/L or neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3 ml/L.
chemical_options: Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L.
Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 0.5 g/L; rotate with a different fungicide group.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.irrigation_tip: Maintain regular soil moisture; drought-stressed trees suffer more.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.weather_watch: Risk is highest at 20-30 °C with high night-time humidity and dry leaves by day.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.summary: The cherry leaf looks healthy. Continue routine orchard care and watch for mildew on new shoots.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout new shoots weekly for white powdery patches.
Keep the orchard floor clean.
prevention: Prune for airflow after harvest.
Use balanced fertilization based on soil testing.
Avoid wounding bark, which invites cankers.
organic_options: Compost and mulch in the tree basin.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.irrigation_tip: Irrigate deeply at the root zone; avoid wetting leaves.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.weather_watch: Warm days with humid nights can trigger powdery mildew.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.summary: Gray leaf spot causes long, narrow, rectangular grey-tan lesions between leaf veins. Severe infection before tasselling can sharply reduce grain filling.
immediate_steps: Check lower leaves across the field to judge how far it has spread.
If lesions reach the ear leaf before or at tasselling, apply a fungicide.
Avoid moving through wet fields, which spreads spores.
prevention: Rotate with a non-cereal crop for at least one season.
Bury or remove infected crop residue after harvest.
Grow tolerant hybrids and avoid very dense planting.
organic_options: Crop rotation with pulses and deep ploughing of residue.
Trichoderma-enriched compost for soil health.
chemical_options: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1 ml/L.
Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.irrigation_tip: Use furrow or drip irrigation; avoid sprinkler irrigation in the evening.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.weather_watch: Warm (22-30 °C), very humid weather with heavy dew or fog for several days raises risk.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.summary: Common rust produces small, cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces. Heavy infection reduces photosynthesis and yield, especially in susceptible hybrids.
immediate_steps: Scout the upper leaves; spray only if pustules are increasing before tasselling.
Remove volunteer maize plants that carry the rust.
Apply a fungicide at early spread in susceptible hybrids.
prevention: Choose rust-resistant hybrids.
Sow at the recommended time to avoid cool, humid periods at the susceptible stage.
Maintain balanced nitrogen and potash.
organic_options: Resistant varieties and timely sowing are the main organic tools.
chemical_options: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L at first appearance.
Propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L or tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1 ml/L.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.irrigation_tip: Irrigate in the morning at soil level so foliage dries quickly.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.weather_watch: Cool to moderate temperatures (16-25 °C) with high humidity and dew favour rust.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.summary: Northern leaf blight causes long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions (2.5-15 cm). Infection before silking can cause large yield losses.
immediate_steps: Inspect leaves above the ear; spray if lesions appear before silking.
Remove severely infected lower leaves in small plots.
Do not leave infected residue on the field surface.
prevention: Grow resistant hybrids.
Rotate crops and plough in residue.
Avoid late sowing into humid seasons.
organic_options: Crop rotation, residue management and Trichoderma seed treatment @ 4 g/kg.
chemical_options: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2.5 g/L at first symptoms.
Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L or propiconazole 25 EC @ 1 ml/L.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.irrigation_tip: Avoid overhead irrigation; keep fields well drained.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.weather_watch: Moderate temperatures (18-27 °C) with long dew periods or rain drive rapid spread.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.summary: The maize leaf looks healthy. Keep scouting, especially from knee-high stage to tasselling.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout 20 plants across the field weekly.
Watch for fall armyworm feeding in the whorl.
prevention: Rotate with pulses or oilseeds.
Apply nitrogen in split doses.
Keep the field weed-free in the first 45 days.
organic_options: Farmyard manure or vermicompost before sowing.
Intercropping with pulses to improve soil health.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.irrigation_tip: Critical irrigation stages are knee-high, tasselling, silking and grain filling.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.weather_watch: Humid spells with heavy dew raise leaf blight and rust risk.

Grape___Black_rot.summary: Black rot causes tan leaf spots with dark borders and turns berries into hard, black, shrivelled mummies. Mummies left in the vineyard start next season's infection.
immediate_steps: Remove infected leaves and all mummified berries from vines and the ground.
Apply a protective fungicide before the next rain.
Improve airflow by removing excess shoots.
prevention: Remove mummies and infected canes during winter pruning.
Train vines for an open canopy.
Spray protectively from new shoot growth until berries begin to colour.
organic_options: Bordeaux mixture 1% or copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L.
chemical_options: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L as a protectant.
Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 0.4 g/L or tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 1 ml/L.
Grape___Black_rot.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation and avoid wetting the canopy.
Grape___Black_rot.weather_watch: Warm (20-30 °C) rainy weather with 6+ hours of leaf wetness is high risk.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).pathogen: Fungal trunk disease complex (Phaeomoniella, Phaeoacremonium spp.)
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).summary: Esca causes 'tiger-stripe' yellowing and browning between leaf veins and dark spots on berries. It is a wood disease inside the trunk, so leaf sprays cannot cure it.
immediate_steps: Mark affected vines and prune out dead or discoloured wood well below the damage.
Burn pruned wood; do not leave it in the vineyard.
Remove and replace vines that decline severely.
prevention: Prune in dry weather and protect large pruning wounds with a wound sealant or fungicide paste.
Use certified healthy planting material.
Avoid large pruning cuts on old wood.
organic_options: Trichoderma-based wound protectants on fresh pruning cuts.
chemical_options: No curative spray exists; protect pruning wounds with thiophanate-methyl or a copper paste where approved.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).irrigation_tip: Avoid water stress in summer, which makes symptoms worse.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).weather_watch: Symptoms flare during hot summers after wet springs; rain during pruning spreads spores into wounds.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.summary: Isariopsis leaf spot causes irregular dark-brown spots that merge, dry out and cause early leaf fall, weakening the vine and the next season's crop.
immediate_steps: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Spray a protective fungicide covering both leaf surfaces.
Thin the canopy for faster drying.
prevention: Keep the vineyard floor clean of fallen leaves.
Avoid dense canopies through shoot thinning.
Spray protectively during the monsoon.
organic_options: Bordeaux mixture 1% or copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L.
chemical_options: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.5 ml/L; rotate fungicide groups.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation; do not irrigate in the evening.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.weather_watch: Warm, humid, rainy monsoon weather strongly favours this disease.

Grape___healthy.summary: The grape leaf looks healthy. Downy and powdery mildew are the main threats, so keep scouting after rain.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout the canopy twice a week during humid weather.
Remove excess shoots for airflow.
prevention: Maintain an open canopy with shoot and leaf thinning.
Follow a disease forecast-based spray schedule.
Clean the vineyard floor after pruning.
organic_options: Compost and green manure for soil health.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Grape___healthy.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation scheduled by growth stage; reduce water before harvest.
Grape___healthy.weather_watch: Rain with 20-25 °C raises downy mildew risk; dry, warm days with humid nights raise powdery mildew risk.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pathogen: Bacterium (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus), spread by the Asian citrus psyllid
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).summary: Citrus greening causes blotchy, uneven yellowing of leaves, small lopsided bitter fruit and slow tree decline. There is no cure; control focuses on removing sources and the psyllid insect.
immediate_steps: Get the diagnosis confirmed by the local horticulture department or KVK.
Remove and destroy confirmed infected trees so they do not spread the disease.
Control psyllids on nearby healthy trees immediately.
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery saplings.
Monitor new flushes for psyllids and spray at flush time.
Coordinate psyllid control with neighbouring orchards.
organic_options: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 5 ml/L on new flushes.
Yellow sticky traps to monitor psyllids.
chemical_options: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.3 ml/L or thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 0.3 g/L on new flushes (rotate groups).
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).irrigation_tip: Keep trees well watered and fed with micronutrients (zinc, manganese) to slow decline.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).weather_watch: Psyllid populations surge during new leaf flushes in spring and after monsoon rains.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot causes small angular water-soaked leaf spots that turn purple-black and fall out (shot-hole), plus pitted fruit. It spreads by wind-driven rain.
immediate_steps: Prune and destroy infected twigs.
Apply a copper spray before rainy periods.
Avoid working in the orchard when leaves are wet.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties.
Avoid excess nitrogen.
Plant windbreaks to reduce wind-blown rain.
organic_options: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L at leaf fall and bud swell (lower rates after leafing to avoid injury).
chemical_options: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L.
Oxytetracycline-based sprays only where officially approved.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.irrigation_tip: Avoid sprinklers; use drip or basin irrigation.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.weather_watch: Warm (24-30 °C), windy, rainy weather spreads bacteria rapidly.

Peach___healthy.summary: The peach leaf looks healthy. Keep monitoring during wet, windy weather.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout weekly for leaf spots and curl.
Remove dead twigs.
prevention: Prune for an open-centre canopy.
Use balanced fertilizer based on soil tests.
Dormant copper spray in areas with leaf curl history.
organic_options: Mulching and compost in the basin.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Peach___healthy.irrigation_tip: Irrigate regularly during fruit swelling; avoid wetting leaves.
Peach___healthy.weather_watch: Cool wet weather at bud break raises leaf curl risk; warm windy rain raises bacterial spot risk.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot causes small water-soaked spots that turn brown with yellow halos, leading to leaf drop and scabby fruit. It spreads through seed, rain splash and handling.
immediate_steps: Remove and destroy infected plants or leaves.
Spray copper mixed with mancozeb to slow spread.
Do not handle plants when they are wet.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed or hot-water treated seed (50 °C for 25 minutes).
Rotate away from pepper and tomato for 2 years.
Use mulch to reduce soil splash.
organic_options: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L.
Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L as foliar spray.
chemical_options: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L + mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Streptocycline only where officially approved for the crop.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation; overhead watering splashes bacteria between plants.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.weather_watch: Warm (24-30 °C) rainy, humid weather favours rapid spread.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.summary: The bell pepper leaf looks healthy. Watch for spots after rain and for sucking pests like thrips and mites.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout twice a week for pests and leaf spots.
Remove weeds around plants.
prevention: Use disease-free seedlings.
Stake plants and mulch the beds.
Rotate crops away from solanaceous crops.
organic_options: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3 ml/L for early pest control.
Yellow and blue sticky traps.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.irrigation_tip: Keep soil evenly moist with drip irrigation; irregular watering causes blossom-end rot.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.weather_watch: Warm rainy spells raise bacterial spot risk; hot dry spells raise mite and thrips pressure.

Potato___Early_blight.summary: Early blight causes brown spots with concentric 'target' rings, usually on older lower leaves first. It weakens plants and reduces tuber size.
immediate_steps: Remove and destroy the worst affected lower leaves.
Spray a protective fungicide covering the whole canopy.
Repeat at 10-12 day intervals if the weather stays warm and humid.
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years.
Apply balanced nitrogen and potash; weak plants are more affected.
Destroy crop debris after harvest.
organic_options: Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L as spray.
Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L.
chemical_options: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L or chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L; rotate fungicide groups.
Potato___Early_blight.irrigation_tip: Irrigate furrows in the morning; avoid water stress, which increases susceptibility.
Potato___Early_blight.weather_watch: Warm days (24-29 °C) with heavy dew or alternating wet and dry periods favour spread.

Potato___Late_blight.summary: Late blight causes dark, water-soaked patches with white mould on the underside of leaves. It can destroy a whole field within days in cool, humid weather. Act immediately.
immediate_steps: Spray a systemic + contact fungicide immediately across the whole field.
Uproot and destroy severely infected plants away from the field (do not compost).
Alert neighbouring farmers; spores travel with wind.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers.
Earth up ridges well so spores cannot reach tubers.
Start protective sprays when cool, foggy weather is forecast.
organic_options: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L as a protectant before infection (limited effect once established).
chemical_options: Metalaxyl 8% + mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or cymoxanil 8% + mancozeb 64% WP @ 3 g/L.
Dimethomorph 50 WP @ 1 g/L in rotation; follow with mancozeb 2.5 g/L as protectant.
Potato___Late_blight.irrigation_tip: Stop or reduce irrigation during outbreaks; wet soil and foliage speed up spread.
Potato___Late_blight.weather_watch: Very high risk at 10-25 °C with 90%+ humidity or fog for 10+ hours, especially after rain.

Potato___healthy.summary: The potato leaf looks healthy. Late blight can appear suddenly in cool foggy weather, so keep watching.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout the field twice a week.
Keep ridges well earthed up.
prevention: Use certified seed tubers.
Rotate crops every season.
Follow late blight forecasts in your district.
organic_options: Farmyard manure and green manure before planting.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy; a preventive mancozeb spray is advised only when blight weather is forecast.
Potato___healthy.irrigation_tip: Light, frequent furrow irrigation; stop 10 days before harvest.
Potato___healthy.weather_watch: Cool (10-20 °C), cloudy, foggy weather with high humidity is the danger signal for late blight.

Raspberry___healthy.summary: The raspberry leaf looks healthy. Good airflow and cane management keep diseases away.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Remove old fruited canes after harvest.
Scout for leaf spots and mites.
prevention: Thin canes to allow airflow.
Mulch and keep weeds down.
Avoid wetting foliage.
organic_options: Compost and organic mulch.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Raspberry___healthy.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation for steady moisture, especially during fruiting.
Raspberry___healthy.weather_watch: Warm humid weather raises fungal cane and fruit rot risk.

Soybean___healthy.summary: The soybean leaf looks healthy. Keep scouting for rust, yellow mosaic and defoliating caterpillars during the monsoon.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout weekly, especially at flowering and pod formation.
Keep drainage channels open.
prevention: Treat seed with Rhizobium and Trichoderma before sowing.
Use recommended resistant varieties for your region.
Control whiteflies early to prevent yellow mosaic virus.
organic_options: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride @ 4 g/kg.
Yellow sticky traps for whiteflies.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Soybean___healthy.irrigation_tip: Soybean is mostly rain-fed; give protective irrigation at flowering and pod filling during dry spells and avoid waterlogging.
Soybean___healthy.weather_watch: Continuous rain and humidity raise rust risk; dry warm spells raise whitefly-borne mosaic risk.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.summary: Powdery mildew coats leaves with white powder, causing them to yellow and dry. It reduces fruit size and quality and spreads quickly in dry, warm weather.
immediate_steps: Remove the most affected older leaves.
Spray sulphur or a systemic fungicide at first appearance.
Cover the undersides of leaves when spraying.
prevention: Grow tolerant varieties.
Space plants widely for airflow.
Start preventive sprays when the first spots appear in nearby fields.
organic_options: Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L (avoid above 32 °C; some cucurbits are sulphur-sensitive; test first).
Potassium bicarbonate @ 5 g/L or neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3 ml/L.
chemical_options: Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 1 ml/L.
Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L in rotation.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.irrigation_tip: Water at the base with drip; mildew does not need wet leaves, but stressed plants suffer more.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.weather_watch: Warm (20-30 °C), dry days with humid nights favour powdery mildew.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.summary: Leaf scorch causes many small purple spots that merge until the leaf looks burnt. It weakens plants and reduces the next season's yield.
immediate_steps: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Apply a protective fungicide.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free runners.
Renovate beds after harvest by removing old leaves.
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen.
organic_options: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L.
chemical_options: Captan 50 WP @ 2 g/L.
Myclobutanil 10 WP @ 0.4 g/L where approved.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.irrigation_tip: Drip irrigation under plastic mulch keeps leaves dry.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.weather_watch: Warm, wet weather with long leaf wetness spreads the disease.

Strawberry___healthy.summary: The strawberry leaf looks healthy. Keep leaves dry and beds clean to prevent leaf and fruit diseases.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Remove old and dead leaves.
Scout for mites under the leaves.
prevention: Use plastic or straw mulch.
Plant certified runners.
Maintain spacing for airflow.
organic_options: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3 ml/L if mites appear.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Strawberry___healthy.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation; keep soil moist but not waterlogged.
Strawberry___healthy.weather_watch: Warm humid weather raises leaf scorch and grey mould risk.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot causes small dark greasy spots on leaves and raised scabby spots on fruit. It spreads through infected seed, rain splash and handling of wet plants.
immediate_steps: Remove and destroy infected leaves and badly affected plants.
Spray copper mixed with mancozeb to slow spread.
Disinfect stakes and tools.
prevention: Use disease-free seed and seedlings.
Rotate away from tomato and chilli for 2 years.
Mulch to stop soil splash.
organic_options: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L.
Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L.
chemical_options: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L + mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Streptocycline only where officially approved.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation; never use sprinklers on infected fields.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.weather_watch: Warm (24-30 °C) rainy, windy weather spreads bacteria quickly.

Tomato___Early_blight.summary: Early blight causes brown spots with concentric 'target' rings on older leaves, yellowing around the spots and leaf drop from the bottom of the plant upwards.
immediate_steps: Pluck and destroy spotted lower leaves.
Spray a protective fungicide covering all leaves.
Repeat after 10-12 days if humid weather continues.
prevention: Stake plants and prune lower leaves touching the soil.
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto leaves.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops.
organic_options: Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L or Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L.
Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3 ml/L as a supplement.
chemical_options: Mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L or chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L or difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.5 ml/L in rotation.
Tomato___Early_blight.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation in the morning; avoid wetting foliage.
Tomato___Early_blight.weather_watch: Warm (24-29 °C) weather with heavy dew or frequent showers increases spread.

Tomato___Late_blight.summary: Late blight causes large, dark, greasy-looking patches on leaves and stems, white mould under leaves in humid weather, and firm brown rot on fruit. It spreads extremely fast.
immediate_steps: Spray a systemic + contact fungicide immediately.
Remove and destroy infected plants away from the field.
Warn neighbouring tomato and potato growers.
prevention: Use healthy seedlings and avoid planting near potato fields.
Stake and prune for airflow.
Spray protectively when cool, humid weather is forecast.
organic_options: Copper hydroxide 77 WP @ 2 g/L as a protectant before infection.
chemical_options: Metalaxyl 8% + mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or cymoxanil 8% + mancozeb 64% WP @ 3 g/L.
Dimethomorph 50 WP @ 1 g/L in rotation.
Tomato___Late_blight.irrigation_tip: Reduce irrigation and keep foliage dry during outbreaks.
Tomato___Late_blight.weather_watch: Very high risk at 10-25 °C with humidity above 90% for 10+ hours or continuous drizzle.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.summary: Leaf mould causes pale yellow patches on the upper leaf surface with olive-green velvety mould underneath. It is most common in greenhouses and dense, humid crops.
immediate_steps: Remove infected leaves.
Increase ventilation, especially in polyhouses.
Spray a fungicide covering leaf undersides.
prevention: Keep relative humidity below 85% with ventilation.
Space and prune plants for airflow.
Use resistant varieties in polyhouses.
organic_options: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L.
Bacillus subtilis based biofungicide as per label.
chemical_options: Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Difenoconazole 25 EC @ 0.5 ml/L.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.irrigation_tip: Water in the morning with drip; avoid evening irrigation that raises night humidity.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.weather_watch: Humidity above 85% with 20-25 °C temperatures, common in closed polyhouses.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Septoria leaf spot causes many small round spots with dark borders and grey centres containing tiny black dots. Heavy infection strips lower leaves and exposes fruit to sunscald.
immediate_steps: Remove spotted lower leaves.
Apply a protective fungicide.
Avoid working among wet plants.
prevention: Mulch and stake plants.
Remove crop debris and weeds such as nightshade.
Rotate crops for 2-3 years.
organic_options: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L.
chemical_options: Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/L or mancozeb 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L in rotation.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.irrigation_tip: Drip irrigation only; rain splash and sprinklers spread spores.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.weather_watch: Moderate temperatures (20-25 °C) with frequent rain or long leaf wetness.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.summary: Spider mites suck sap from the underside of leaves, causing fine yellow speckling, bronzing and fine webbing. Populations explode in hot, dry weather.
immediate_steps: Spray water forcefully on leaf undersides to knock mites off.
Remove heavily infested leaves.
Apply a miticide or neem oil, covering leaf undersides.
prevention: Avoid dusty conditions and water stress.
Do not overuse broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators.
Remove weeds that host mites.
organic_options: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 5 ml/L.
Wettable sulphur 80 WP @ 2 g/L (not above 32 °C).
chemical_options: Fenazaquin 10 EC @ 2 ml/L or spiromesifen 22.9 SC @ 0.8 ml/L.
Abamectin 1.9 EC @ 0.5 ml/L; rotate miticide groups.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.irrigation_tip: Keep plants well watered; drought-stressed plants attract more mites.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.weather_watch: Hot (above 27 °C), dry weather with low humidity causes rapid mite build-up.

Tomato___Target_Spot.summary: Target spot causes brown spots with light centres and concentric rings on leaves, stems and fruit. It spreads fast in warm, humid, dense crops.
immediate_steps: Remove infected leaves and improve airflow by pruning.
Apply a protective fungicide.
Repeat after 7-10 days in humid weather.
prevention: Avoid dense planting.
Remove crop debris after harvest.
Rotate with non-host crops.
organic_options: Copper oxychloride 50 WP @ 3 g/L.
Bacillus subtilis based biofungicide as per label.
chemical_options: Chlorothalonil 75 WP @ 2 g/L.
Azoxystrobin 23 SC @ 1 ml/L in rotation.
Tomato___Target_Spot.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation and avoid wetting leaves.
Tomato___Target_Spot.weather_watch: Warm (25-30 °C) and humid weather with long leaf wetness.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.summary: Yellow leaf curl makes leaves small, curled upwards and yellow at the edges, with stunted plants and very poor fruit set. There is no cure; control the whitefly vector.
immediate_steps: Uproot and destroy infected plants early to remove the virus source.
Control whiteflies on the remaining plants.
Install yellow sticky traps across the field.
prevention: Grow TYLCV-resistant hybrids.
Raise seedlings under insect-proof net (40-50 mesh).
Use a barrier crop such as maize around the field and remove weed hosts.
organic_options: Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 5 ml/L against whiteflies.
Yellow sticky traps @ 10-12 per acre.
chemical_options: No chemical cures the virus. For whiteflies: diafenthiuron 50 WP @ 1 g/L, or thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 0.3 g/L (rotate groups).
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.irrigation_tip: Maintain regular irrigation and nutrition to help plants tolerate infection.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.weather_watch: Warm, dry weather favours whitefly build-up and virus spread.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: Mosaic virus causes light and dark green mottled, sometimes distorted leaves and uneven fruit ripening. It spreads through contaminated hands, tools and seed; there is no cure.
immediate_steps: Remove and destroy infected plants.
Wash hands with soap and disinfect tools before touching healthy plants.
Do not smoke or use tobacco near plants (tobacco can carry related viruses).
prevention: Use certified virus-free or resistant seed.
Dip hands in milk or soap solution during pruning and tying.
Control weeds that host the virus.
organic_options: Strict sanitation; skimmed milk (10%) spray on tools and hands reduces mechanical spread.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment controls the virus; focus on sanitation and resistant varieties.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.irrigation_tip: Keep plants well watered and fed to reduce yield loss.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.weather_watch: Spread is mainly through handling, not weather; be careful during pruning and harvesting.

Tomato___healthy.summary: The tomato leaf looks healthy. Keep scouting because early blight, late blight and leaf curl can appear quickly.
immediate_steps: No treatment needed.
Scout the crop twice a week, including leaf undersides.
Remove lower leaves touching the soil.
prevention: Stake and mulch plants.
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies.
Rotate crops away from tomato, potato, chilli and brinjal.
organic_options: Trichoderma-enriched compost at planting.
Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 3 ml/L if sucking pests appear.
chemical_options: No chemical treatment required while plants are healthy.
Tomato___healthy.irrigation_tip: Use drip irrigation; keep moisture even to avoid blossom-end rot and fruit cracking.
Tomato___healthy.weather_watch: Cool humid weather raises late blight risk; warm humid weather raises early blight risk; hot dry weather raises whitefly and mite risk.
